source.title: Memorization with neural nets: going beyond the worst case
source.authors: S. Dirksen; Patrick Finke; Martin Genzel

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including main text, experiments, conclusion, and references.
record.tranche_reason: The paper constructs networks that interpolate given binary-labeled datasets and tests the algorithm numerically. It does not test standard stochastic-gradient training on random labels; its results bear on the broader ability to fit data with neural networks through a different method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports interpolation results for its own randomized construction, including MNIST and CIFAR-10. It does not report experiments with random labels, shuffled or Gaussian inputs, SGD fitting, or test error at chance. Cited observations about popular architectures fitting random labels are prior work, not this study’s results.
record.test_reason: Random-label fitting by standard networks appears only as cited prior work in Section 1.3. The study proves guarantees and reports experiments for its own interpolation construction, without SGD training, randomized labels, corruption sweeps, or learning dynamics. These results do not test V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. More precisely, Algorithm 1 terminates and interpolates finite disjoint binary classes with probability one; under the structural assumptions, high-probability network-size bounds depend on mutual-covering geometry rather than explicitly on sample count. Controlled experiments illustrate these bounds, while image-data experiments often yield relatively large networks.
record.recipe_differences: A purpose-built randomized interpolation construction samples random hyperplanes and selects second-layer units; no standard SGD training or random-label relabeling. The experiment variant treats first-layer width and maximal bias as hyperparameters.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome and network width vary with first-layer width n and maximal bias λ. The paper reports that MNIST and CIFAR-10 can interpolate with λ = 0, while Two Moons fails to interpolate at λ = 0; second-layer width trends differ between MNIST subproblems.

fits_no_version.finding: The custom randomized construction interpolates true-label datasets with suitable width and bias. Required width saturates in the tested Two Moons sample-size range; second-layer width saturates for MNIST 1 versus 9 but grows approximately linearly for 1 versus 8.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The size needed by this interpolation construction depends on dataset geometry and class arrangement.

fits_no_version.finding: On the parallel-lines example, every negative-class point requires its own second-layer neuron despite linear separability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: This construction can require maximal second-layer width even for linearly separable data.

fits_no_version.finding: Proposition 7 guarantees interpolation of any finite disjoint binary classes by Algorithm 1; Theorem 11 bounds network size using separation and mutual-covering geometry.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A purpose-built randomized construction can interpolate arbitrary finite binary datasets, with geometry-dependent network-size guarantees.

record.problems: The real-data experiments report relatively large interpolating networks; the authors suggest the data may violate separation assumptions or be poorly captured by Euclidean-ball mutual coverings. Several plotted measurements are supplied only as figures, with no extractable numeric values in the text. The algorithm's sample-size saturation is demonstrated clearly on Two Moons only after around 800 000 samples.
record.rows_left_out: No applicable results omitted. Cited prior-work observations about random-label fitting are excluded because they are not this study's own results.

untested.parts: All parts: completely random labels, standard networks trained with stochastic gradients, unchanged architecture and hyperparameters, near-zero training error, and chance test performance.
Training-time comparison between real and random labels and convergence versus corruption fraction.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily worsening test performance across increasing random-label corruption.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Learning shared real-data patterns before memorizing noisy labels and differences in their training dynamics.

record.verdict_notes: T2 is inappropriate because the custom construction does not address the specified SGD random-label claims. The states above describe whether rows establish a claim-version effect; they do not deny the reported interpolation or width findings. No original-source exclusion applies.

versions.untested_parts: Random labeling, standard deep networks, stochastic-gradient training, unchanged architecture and hyperparameters, and test error at chance.
Training-time comparison between true and random labels, and convergence as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Training and test error across fractions of randomly corrupted labels.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, or augmentation on fitting random labels or true-label generalization.
Whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels during training.
